description: We are a team of four student engineers — Akhmet, Ali, Sergazy, and Miras — driven by a passion for competitive programming, web development, and space tech. For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, we combine strong algorithmic problem-solving with data analytics to build intuitive, high-performance web tools for exploring space data.
summary:
Pluto was found in 1930 by blinking two photographs and spotting one dot that moved. NASA's SPHEREx now photographs the whole sky in 102 infrared colours every six months, but comparing even one spot today means downloading about 3 GB and aligning images by hand. InfraBlink is a free website that does this in under a minute in any browser: type a position, and it pulls every real SPHEREx exposure of that spot from NASA's archive, reads only the pixels it needs (about 30 MB instead of 3 GB), aligns and stacks them by survey pass, subtracts them, and measures what moved, what changed and what its spectrum says it is.

We tested it on all five challenge targets and on Pluto: Barnard's Star moved 10.5″ in a year (catalogue 10.3″); WISE 0855−0714, invisible in one exposure, appears in the stacks; Pluto is found 1.5″ (a quarter of a pixel) from the JPL prediction. Then we asked the honest question: could SPHEREx find Planet X? Our calculator shows a typical Planet Nine is 12.6× too faint for one pass, and an injection test with fake movers hidden in real data proves our search reaches AB 18.8 (theory 18.9) with 0.3% false alarms. Finally we turned the site into a classroom: missions with automatic answer checking, ten video lessons and 45-minute lesson plans, in English, Kazakh and Russian.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

• Blink viewer: any sky position (coordinates or a name). Every SPHEREx exposure of that spot in time order, survey passes stacked, and difference images where a moving object becomes a blue (then) / orange (now) pair.

• "Did it move?": click a source and its position is measured in every exposure and compared with the catalogue prediction, including Earth's parallax.

• Spectral fingerprint: the 0.75–5 µm spectrum of a source from all its exposures, with neighbour stars from Gaia DR3 fitted and removed, compared with six templates (Sun-like star, red dwarf, cold methane brown dwarf, galaxy, asteroid, cold planet).

• Track an object: NASA/IPAC's Moving Object Search Tool lists every SPHEREx exposure of Pluto (or any asteroid or comet); the site follows the body, stacks along its orbit and checks it against JPL Horizons.

• Sky map: the whole sky with real SPHEREx footprints coloured by date, a "Play the survey" animation, the Planet Nine probability region from Brown & Batygin (2021) and today's positions of the extreme TNOs.

• Could SPHEREx see Planet X?: a physics calculator (mass–radius, reflected sunlight plus thermal emission, SPHEREx 5σ depth) with every formula shown.

• Injection test: fake moving point sources planted into the real stacked images and searched with the site's own detector, giving completeness and false-alarm rate.

• Practice and Classroom: student missions with automatic answer checking, teacher-made missions as one link, ten narrated video lessons and three 45-minute lesson plans.

• English, Kazakh and Russian; every view is a shareable link.

HOW IT WORKS

The browser asks NASA/IPAC IRSA (Simple Image Access) which SPHEREx Level-2 exposures cover the spot, then reads only the needed bytes of each 62 MB file from NASA's public cloud copy with HTTP Range requests. It applies each exposure's own TAN-SIP calibration, re-projects onto one north-up grid, stacks with sigma clipping, and measures positions and fluxes. Tiny serverless functions only relay requests to IRSA, JPL, CDS and Gaia because those services do not send CORS headers. If an archive is down, saved copies of its answers keep the built-in examples, missions and Pluto working.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Anyone with a browser can now check what SPHEREx saw at any spot, without installing software or downloading gigabytes. Students repeat the method that found Pluto on real, current NASA data and learn why a scientist must also know what they could not have found. Teachers get ready lessons in three languages. For Planet X, the site gives an honest, reproducible answer: the method works, a deeper survey is needed.

TOOLS

Plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS (no frameworks, no build step), Vercel serverless functions, NASA's public AWS copy of SPHEREx, IRSA SIA and MOST, JPL Horizons and Small-Body Database, Gaia DR3, CDS SIMBAD/Sesame. Video lessons: screen recordings of the site, FFmpeg, Kokoro text-to-speech.
projectRefs: Brown & Batygin 2021, The Orbit of Planet Nine
